text.text: Your eye care practice in one place. Start with Exams for today, call patients under Patients whose recall is due, and keep Optical orders moving. Operational tracking only; exam records and prescriptions stay in your clinical system.
Most patients need an eye exam every year or two, and many forget until something goes wrong. A steady recall routine keeps the schedule full and catches problems early.

text.text: Vision plans pay for exams and glasses on their own schedule, often every 12 or 24 months, with allowances for frames and lenses. Checking before the visit avoids surprises at the optical counter.
For every patient on tomorrow's schedule
Check eligibility on the plan's portal: exam covered, frame allowance, lens benefit, contact lens allowance and the copays.
Note the date the plan next covers frames in
If the patient comes for a medical reason (red eye, diabetes, floaters, glaucoma), the visit may be billed to their medical insurance instead. Ask for that card too.
Insurance card scanned, subscriber and date of birth confirmed
Patient told what the plan covers for glasses or contacts today
Show frames within the allowance first, then upgrades with their extra cost.
Lens add-ons (anti-glare, blue filter, thinner lenses, photochromic) are usually partly covered; explain the patient's share for each.

cells.text: What it means at the counter
Book on or after the anniversary, not a week early
Offer a second pair at a discount instead
Many plans cover one or the other in a benefit period
Patient pays and submits the receipt; give an itemized receipt

text.text: A routine check of how well someone sees is a vision visit. A visit for an eye problem (infection, injury, flashes and floaters, diabetes, glaucoma follow-up) is usually medical. Decide at booking, tell the patient which card you will bill, and write it on the exam page so the claim goes to the right place.
Submit the exam and materials claim the day of the visit, with the lab job number for glasses. Check unpaid claims every two weeks.
Kingsley's plan renewed 30 days ago. The front desk sees it during the morning check, calls him, and books his exam and frames for the same visit.
Glasses are measured, ordered, checked and fitted. Each step has a chance to go wrong, and patients remember a late or wrong pair far longer than a good exam.
Help the patient pick a frame that fits: size, bridge, temple length and lens type. Progressives need enough frame height.
Measure pupillary distance and, for progressives, fitting heights.

The frame board is the store window. Too many slow frames tie up cash; gaps in popular styles and sizes lose sales.
Count each frame on the board and in the drawers and update

Kids' frames that are sturdy, with spring hinges.

Frames that have not sold in six months move to a sale tray or go back to the vendor if your agreement allows returns. Write the date you moved them on the frame's page.
Frame tagged with price and size before it goes on the board

Keep a simple rule, for example retail at two and a half to three times cost, and apply it consistently. Patients compare prices; a frame that costs more than a similar one on the board needs a clear reason.
Board layout refreshed with new arrivals at eye level
Children's section checked for gaps before school starts
Returns sent back before the vendor's deadline
One optician owns the board: counts, reorders, returns and pricing. Everyone else tells them when a frame sells out or a patient asks for something you do not carry.
The children's Tumble frame is down to two on hand with back-to-school exams booked all next week. The optician reorders six in the two most common sizes.
The front of an eye care practice: today's exams, patients due back, what each vision plan covers, frames on the board and glasses at the lab. Exam records stay in your clinical system.
